title: One Supernova, Five Images, and a New Way to Measure the Universe
hook: A gravitational lens split a colossal exploding star into five copies. Timing the gaps between them gives a fresh, ladder-free measurement of how fast the cosmos expands.
key_points: SN 2025wny is a superluminous Type I supernova at redshift z = 2.015, lensed by two foreground galaxies into five resolved images.
It is the first strongly lensed superluminous supernova ever found, and the first galaxy-scale lensed supernova with both photometric and spectroscopic time delays.
Because the five images travel different path lengths, the delays between their light curves encode the Hubble constant directly.
HST and JWST follow-up yields H0 = 66.7 (+7.6/-6.3) km/s/Mpc for isothermal lens models, or 70.8 (+8.2/-6.1) with freer density slopes.
The same data give the most detailed rest-frame UV view of any superluminous supernova, hinting at a non-standard power source.
content_html: In 2026 astronomers caught a spectacular coincidence: a superluminous supernova exploding 10 billion light-years away, at redshift 2.015, with two foreground galaxies sitting almost exactly in the line of sight. Their combined gravity bent the light into five separate images of the same explosion — the first time this has happened to a superluminous supernova, and a rare gift for cosmology.
extra_html:
The reason it matters is timing. Each image's light takes a slightly different route around the lensing galaxies, so the same explosion shows up at Earth on five different dates. The size of those gaps depends on the geometry of the lens and on how fast the universe is expanding — which means a lensed supernova measures the Hubble constant in one step, without relying on the usual chain of calibrated distance indicators.

A team led by Ariel Goobar and collaborators (Stockholm University and partners) reported HST and JWST follow-up of SN 2025wny in a series of arXiv papers in August 2026. Modeling the two lens galaxies as elliptical power-law mass distributions plus external shear, Edvard Mörtsell and colleagues derive H0 = 66.7 (+7.6/−6.3) km/s/Mpc for isothermal profiles, rising to 70.8 (+8.2/−6.1) when the density slopes are allowed to vary. The uncertainties are still large, so this single system doesn't settle the Hubble tension — but it demonstrates the method on a new class of object, and the companion analysis by Maggie Li and Lin Yan notes the supernova's light curve may need a hybrid or non-standard power source, making it a reference spectrum for the many high-redshift superluminous supernovae that Rubin and Roman are expected to find.

flashcards.prompt: How does a gravitationally lensed supernova measure the Hubble constant?
flashcards.back_html: Each of its multiple images takes a different path through the lens, so the same explosion arrives at different times. Those time delays depend on the expansion rate, giving H0 without climbing the usual distance ladder.

flashcards.prompt: What makes SN 2025wny unusual among lensed supernovae?

choices.text: It is the first strongly lensed superluminous supernova, split into five resolved images
It is the closest supernova ever observed, inside the Milky Way
It is the first supernova detected purely in gravitational waves

flashcards.explanation_html: Lensed supernovae are already rare; SN 2025wny is the first of the superluminous class, and its five images allow both photometric and spectroscopic time-delay measurements.

flashcards.prompt: Why do the reported H0 values shift depending on the lens model?
flashcards.back_html: The time delays only give H0 once you know how mass is distributed in the lensing galaxies. Assuming isothermal profiles gives about 66.7 km/s/Mpc; letting the density slopes vary freely shifts it to about 70.8, with larger error bars.
